question: What is a dosage form in pharmacology?

options.A: The exact time interval between drug doses
options.B: The physical presentation of a drug product
options.C: The chemical formula of the active ingredient
options.D: The maximum safe blood concentration of a drug

explanation: A dosage form refers to the physical shape and composition in which a medication is manufactured for patient use. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why do manufacturers produce medications in different physical forms?

options.A: To ensure safe and effective delivery to the body
options.B: To make all drugs taste identical for pediatric patients
options.C: To eliminate the need for liver metabolism completely
options.D: To ensure every drug can be crushed into powder

explanation: Different formulations protect the active drug, control absorption rates, and match the intended route of administration. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h1)

question: What happens when an enteric-coated tablet is crushed before administration?

options.A: The tablet turns into a liquid suspension automatically
options.B: The drug dissolves much slower than intended in the body
options.C: The protective coating is destroyed and absorption is altered
options.D: The medication becomes completely inactive in the stomach

explanation: Crushing destroys the special layer meant to protect the stomach lining or delay drug release. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h2)

question: A patient with a nasogastric tube refuses to swallow pills and asks you to crush their sustained-release capsule. What is your best action?

options.A: Open the capsule and mix the beads into water for tube feeding
options.B: Crush the capsule contents finely and mix with fruit juice
options.C: Consult the pharmacist or prescriber for an alternative liquid form
options.D: Crush only half of the capsule contents to reduce the dose

explanation: Altering sustained-release or capsule formulations can cause rapid dumping of the total drug dose into the patient's system. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h2)

question: Why are liquid medications absorbed faster than solid tablets?

options.A: They bypass the liver metabolism on the first pass
options.B: They contain higher concentrations of active chemicals
options.C: They react immediately with gastric acid to speed up
options.D: The active drug is already dissolved in a vehicle

explanation: Because the drug is already in solution, the body does not need to spend time breaking down a solid matrix before absorption. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is the correct tool for measuring an exact dose of liquid oral medication for a child?
explanation: Household spoons vary greatly in capacity and lead to inaccurate dosing, whereas calibrated oral syringes ensure precision. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which topical preparation is best suited for dry, thick, and scaly skin lesions?
explanation: Ointments have a heavy oil or grease base that provides prolonged contact time and locks moisture into dry skin. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why should a nurse wear gloves when applying topical creams containing active drugs to a patient?

options.A: To prevent accidental absorption of the medication through the nurse's skin
options.B: To ensure the cream stays warm before touching the patient's body
options.C: To make the application process look more professional in the ward
options.D: To prevent the patient from smelling the strong fragrance of the base

explanation: Topical medications can pass through the stratum corneum of the healthcare provider during application, leading to unintended systemic exposure. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h4)

question: What crucial step must a nurse perform before applying a new transdermal patch?

options.A: Remove the old patch from the patient's skin
options.B: Clean the skin site with concentrated rubbing alcohol
options.C: Warm the new patch over an open flame briefly
options.D: Cover the new patch completely with gauze tape

explanation: Leaving an old patch in place while applying a new one results in an unintended double dose of medication entering the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of using a spacer with a metered-dose inhaler?

options.A: It eliminates the need for the patient to breathe out first
options.B: It slows down medication delivery and improves lung deposition
options.C: It converts the aerosol spray into a safe oral liquid suspension
options.D: It increases the chemical strength of the drug inside the canister

explanation: Spacers trap the medication cloud so the patient can inhale it slowly and deeply, reducing drug deposition in the mouth and throat. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is a primary nursing rule regarding the preparation of medications?

options.A: Never administer a drug that you did not prepare yourself
options.B: Always prepare all ward medications at the start of the shift
options.C: Ask another nurse to sign off on drugs before checking labels
options.D: Let patients help prepare their own IV infusions to save time

explanation: Preparing your own medications ensures full accountability and prevents medication administration errors on the ward. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h6)

question: A doctor writes an unclear drug order on the treatment sheet. What action should you take?

options.A: Omit the medication dose entirely without telling anyone
options.B: Guess the correct dose based on the patient's diagnosis
options.C: Clarify the ambiguous order directly with the prescriber
options.D: Ask a senior ward patient to help interpret the handwriting

explanation: Nurses must never guess ambiguous orders; direct communication with the prescriber prevents severe medication errors. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T7#GNS125_U2_T7_h6)
